prompt: Where did Thomas Sowell spend much of his childhood after leaving North Carolina, before later earning a PhD in economics?

choices.text: Harlem, New York City
Chicago's South Side
Atlanta's Sweet Auburn
Washington, D.C.'s Anacostia

explain: Sowell was born in Gastonia, North Carolina, and moved with his family to Harlem as a child. Hoover's fellow profile dates the birth to June 30, 1930, names his father Henry, who died before he was born, and his mother Willie, who gave him to his great-aunt Molly. His first memories were a wooden house in Charlotte on an unpaved street, with no electricity or running water. The family moved to Harlem when he was eight, he later entered Stuyvesant High School and dropped out, and he delivered telegrams for Western Union before leaving home at sixteen. [Hoover fellow profile](https://www.hoover.org/news/fellow-profile-thomas-sowell)
source: Hoover Institution, Fellow Profile: Thomas Sowell, February 19, 2021, https://www.hoover.org/news/fellow-profile-thomas-sowell

prompt: In A Conflict of Visions, Sowell's constrained vision of human nature is closest to which claim?

choices.text: People are blank slates, so expert planners can redesign society toward moral perfection
Only genetic determinism explains political disagreement
Markets always fail, so unconstrained reason must replace prices
People are limited and self-interested, so politics should emphasize trade-offs, incentives, and institutional checks

explain: The constrained vision treats human nature as imperfect and hard to remake. In A Conflict of Visions, Sowell takes Adam Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) and The Wealth of Nations as pictures of that vision: moral and economic benefits come from incentives and trade-offs, not from remaking man, and he quotes Edmund Burke on "a radical infirmity in all human contrivances" and Alexander Hamilton in The Federalist Papers on the imperfection of man. He sets William Godwin's Enquiry Concerning Political Justice (1793) against Smith, and the Marquis de Condorcet with Godwin, because they treat selfishness as something reason can dispel and look for solutions rather than trade-offs. He also pairs Thomas Paine with Burke, and later John Kenneth Galbraith with Friedrich Hayek. [A Conflict of Visions](https://archive.org/download/hybridphilosophy-collection/A-Conflict-of-Visions_-Idealogical-Origi-Thomas-Sowell.pdf)
source: Thomas Sowell, A Conflict of Visions (1987), archive text, https://archive.org/download/hybridphilosophy-collection/A-Conflict-of-Visions_-Idealogical-Origi-Thomas-Sowell.pdf

prompt: Sowell's recurring line about policy is best paraphrased as:

choices.text: Good intentions are a sufficient success metric
If voters demand a solution, economics must deliver one
There are no solutions, only trade-offs
Every social problem has one correct technical fix

explain: In the tragic or constrained vision he describes, suffering and scarcity are not abolished by a program. In a 2004 column he answered a listener who demanded his solution by saying, "There are no solutions," only trade-offs, and that voters can demand square circles without getting them. He names the National Housing Act of 1937 as the federal entry into public housing, a 1909 Washington survey that found people spending just under 18 percent of income on housing, and coastal California, where open-space laws, rent control, and environmental red tape block building. He also points to public-housing projects later demolished amid crime, drugs, and single-parent families, and to Howard Husock's America's Trillion-Dollar Housing Mistake. [Housing Hurdles: The Solution?](https://capitalismmagazine.com/2004/02/housing-hurdles-the-solution/)
source: Thomas Sowell, "Housing Hurdles: The Solution?," Capitalism Magazine, February 5, 2004, https://capitalismmagazine.com/2004/02/housing-hurdles-the-solution/

prompt: In Basic Economics, what does Sowell emphasize as a common result of rent control that keeps rents artificially low?

choices.text: Prices stop mattering because demand no longer responds to price
Housing shortages, waiting lists, and often deterioration of rental stock
Permanent surpluses of brand-new luxury apartments
Construction booms because builders earn more under the cap

explain: Holding price below the market level raises quantity demanded and reduces quantity supplied. In the revised and expanded edition of Basic Economics, Sowell names the cases. Under wartime U.S. rent control there was a housing shortage even though there was no less housing space per person than before the war, and when rent control ended the shortage quickly disappeared. In Sweden, less than one-fourth of unmarried adults had their own housing units in 1940, before rent control, and just over half did by 1975, with longer waits for housing; after repeal a surplus appeared and private developers began building. Nine years after the end of World War II, not a single new building had been built in Melbourne, because rent control made building unprofitable. Studies of rent control in the United States, England, and France found rent-controlled housing deteriorated far more often than housing that was not under rent control. See [Basic Economics](https://archive.org/stream/BasicEconomicsACommonSenseGuideToTheEconomy/Sowell%20Basic%20Economics%20A%20Citizen%27s%20Guide%20to%20the%20Economy_djvu.txt).
source: Thomas Sowell, Basic Economics: A Citizen's Guide to the Economy, revised and expanded edition (Basic Books, 2004), https://archive.org/stream/BasicEconomicsACommonSenseGuideToTheEconomy/Sowell%20Basic%20Economics%20A%20Citizen%27s%20Guide%20to%20the%20Economy_djvu.txt

prompt: What is a central theme of Intellectuals and Society?

choices.text: Idea workers can heavily shape public opinion and policy while facing little personal accountability when ideas fail
Only STEM PhDs should vote
Intellectuals have almost no influence in democracies
Universities should be abolished because books are obsolete

explain: Sowell defines intellectuals as people whose work centers on ideas. In the January 5, 2010 column introducing Intellectuals and Society, he says journalists, teachers, legislative staffers, and judges' clerks spread those ideas, and that intellectuals are judged by whether the ideas sound good, not by whether they work. He contrasts the Wright brothers and the people who conquered polio, who were judged by tangible results, with Karl Marx's ideas, which he says cost whole generations and millions of lives. He adds that distinguished Western intellectuals in the 1930s praised the Soviet Union while millions starved and others were sent to slave-labor camps, and urged their own countries to disarm while Hitler armed Germany. [Intellectuals and Society](https://townhall.com/columnists/thomassowell/2010/01/05/intellectuals_and_society)
source: Thomas Sowell, "Intellectuals and Society," Townhall, January 5, 2010, https://townhall.com/columnists/thomassowell/2010/01/05/intellectuals_and_society

prompt: Discrimination and Disparities mainly pushes readers to reject which automatic inference?

choices.text: That discrimination has never existed anywhere
That first-born children never have advantages
That markets always equalize all group averages overnight
That unequal group outcomes by themselves prove discrimination was the sole or primary cause

explain: Sowell argues disparities have many causes, including ones that are not discrimination. Discrimination can matter, but seeing a gap is not enough to infer that only discrimination produced it. In his 17 July 1998 Hoover essay he names cases that are not a single discrimination story. The median age of Jews in the United States was 20 years older than the median age of Puerto Ricans, so the groups could not be equally represented in jobs that take long experience, in retirement homes, or in sports. The Chinese minority, about 5 percent of Indonesia, owned an estimated four-fifths of the capital. In the 1960s the Chinese minority in Malaysia earned more than a hundred times as many engineering degrees as the Malay majority. In Nigeria, people in the northern provinces were 9 percent of the students at the University of Ibadan and 2 percent of Nigerians studying abroad. See [Race, Culture, and Equality](https://www.hoover.org/research/race-culture-and-equality).
source: Thomas Sowell, "Race, Culture, and Equality," Hoover Institution, 17 July 1998, from Commonwealth Club remarks on 18 June 1998, https://www.hoover.org/research/race-culture-and-equality

prompt: In Black Rednecks and White Liberals, Sowell's race-versus-culture theme is closest to which claim?

choices.text: Culture never matters once discrimination is mentioned
Only African history can explain Southern white folkways
Cultural patterns, not race as biology, help explain some group behaviors and outcomes, including traits he traces to Southern redneck culture
Genetics alone determine every social outcome

explain: The title essay argues that some patterns often labeled as uniquely black ghetto culture have historical roots in white Southern cultural patterns, and that romanticizing those patterns can be harmful. In a 16 May 2005 column on the book, Sowell names the cases. Speech such as "ax" for "ask" and "acrost" for "across," which he traces to the British regions white Southerners came from. Violence, illegitimacy, lively music and dance, and a highly emotional style of religious oratory, common in that Southern culture and in those parts of Britain, where most people had never seen anyone black. A lack of emphasis on education, with higher illiteracy among antebellum Southern whites than among Northern whites. He also says the remnant of that culture treats belligerence as manly, crudity as cool, and being civilized as "acting white," and that since the 1960s many white liberals have glamorized it as the only authentic black culture. See [Black Rednecks and White Liberals](https://capitalismmagazine.com/2005/05/black-rednecks-and-white-liberals/).
source: Thomas Sowell, "Black Rednecks and White Liberals," Capitalism Magazine, 16 May 2005, https://capitalismmagazine.com/2005/05/black-rednecks-and-white-liberals/ . The book is Black Rednecks and White Liberals (Encounter, 2005), title essay.

prompt: A city caps apartment rents far below market levels to help tenants. Which reaction is most Sowellian?

choices.text: Conclude that demand for housing does not respond to price
Expect shortages, less new rental supply, and pressure to cut maintenance, because price is a signal, not just a number politicians can erase
Assume landlords will build more units once rents are lower
Treat the shortage as proof that rent caps were set too high

explain: Sowell treats prices as conveying scarcities and costs. In Basic Economics he names what a cap does to supply and upkeep. After rent control was instituted in Santa Monica, California, in 1979, building permits declined to less than one-tenth of what they had been five years earlier. In Berkeley, the number of private housing units available to students at the university declined by 31 percent in five years. During eight years of rent control in Washington in the 1970s, the available rental stock fell from just over 199,000 units to just under 176,000. Landlords provide less maintenance and repair because the shortage makes it unnecessary to attract tenants, and within three years after rent control was imposed in Toronto in 1976, 23 percent of all rental units in owner-occupied dwellings were withdrawn from the market. See [Basic Economics](https://archive.org/stream/BasicEconomicsACommonSenseGuideToTheEconomy/Sowell%20Basic%20Economics%20A%20Citizen%27s%20Guide%20to%20the%20Economy_djvu.txt).
source: Thomas Sowell, Basic Economics: A Citizen's Guide to the Economy, revised and expanded edition (Basic Books, 2004), https://archive.org/stream/BasicEconomicsACommonSenseGuideToTheEconomy/Sowell%20Basic%20Economics%20A%20Citizen%27s%20Guide%20to%20the%20Economy_djvu.txt

prompt: After a factory closes, a panel of professors proposes a detailed national plan for every worker's next job. A Sowellian pushback would most likely stress:

choices.text: The knowledge problem: dispersed local information and changing trade-offs are hard for central planners to know as well as prices and individuals do
That professors always know more than markets about every local job match
That unemployment proves prices convey no useful information
That human nature is unlimited, so one blueprint can optimize everyone's path

explain: Sowell emphasizes that useful knowledge is scattered and that prices help coordinate it. A 19 February 2021 Hoover profile quotes the cases that fixed that point for him. Friedrich Hayek's essay "The Use of Knowledge in Society," assigned in Milton Friedman's price-theory course, left an impression of how fragmented knowledge scattered among vast numbers of people shapes decisions in a free market, and that essay became the influence of Knowledge and Decisions. In the summer of 1960, as an intern at the U.S. Department of Labor, he was assigned the sugar industry in Puerto Rico, which the federal minimum wage covered. Unions and experts in the department blamed hurricanes for rising unemployment. He thought the cause might be the mandated minimum wage and asked for statistics on the amount of sugarcane standing in the fields before the hurricane. He recalled the shock in the room: he was asking whether the law helped low-income people, and they were concerned because the law provided one-third of the income of the Department of Labor. See [Fellow Profile: Thomas Sowell](https://www.hoover.org/news/fellow-profile-thomas-sowell).
source: Hoover Institution, "Fellow Profile: Thomas Sowell," Hoover Daily Report, 19 February 2021, https://www.hoover.org/news/fellow-profile-thomas-sowell

Discrimination is impossible by definition
Only genetics can explain gaps, so stop talking about culture or age
Disparities can have many causes. Discrimination is one possible cause, not an automatic proof from the gap alone

A 21 November 2001 column states that same rule and names cases that are not a discrimination finding. The same basketball rules that cover him and Michael Jordan do not give them equal chances. First-born children average higher IQs than later children. Peoples living in the Himalayas did not develop the seafaring skills of people living in the Greek islands, and the Eskimos did not learn to grow pineapples. See [Thanksgiving and fairness](http://www.jewishworldreview.com/cols/sowell112101.asp).

prompt: A pundit says a new program will solve poverty with no serious downsides. Which follow-up questions are most in Sowell's spirit?

choices.text: How quickly can we expand it before measuring results?
Which slogan polls best with donors?
Compared to what? At what cost? What hard evidence?
Who feels the most moral about it?

explain: He frames policy as comparative and empirical. In his August 9, 2005 column on Hiroshima, he writes that much self-righteous nonsense cannot stand three questions: compared to what, at what cost, and what are the hard facts. He applies them to the atomic bombs of August 6, 1945, on Hiroshima and then Nagasaki, set against ordinary bombing of German cities and Tokyo and against the planned 1946 invasion of Japan. He cites Pacific island fighting in which thousands of Japanese troops died and only a few dozen were captured, wounded soldiers who detonated grenades when a corpsman approached, and kamikaze pilots. [Trashing our history: Hiroshima](http://www.jewishworldreview.com/cols/sowell080905.asp)

prompt: A celebrated social theory fails in practice, but its academic champions keep promoting it and blame implementation, not the idea. Intellectuals and Society would most likely highlight:

choices.text: That empirical track records are irrelevant to social ideas
Weak accountability: idea workers often face little personal cost when theories produce bad results, so evidence may not revise the vision
That failure proves the theory needed even more funding only
That intellectuals never influence democratic opinion

explain: A core claim is that intellectuals shape climates of opinion yet often are not forced to pay for disastrous prescriptions the way market actors are. In the same day's second column, Sowell says academic freedom and freedom of the press shield idea workers even from a loss of credibility. He asks who blames Rachel Carson after writings against DDT led to bans and a resurgence of malaria that killed millions in tropical countries. He names Woodrow Wilson, the only president with a Ph.D., whose war to end wars and self-determination of peoples were followed by worse regimes in Russia and Germany, by Hitler picking off the small states carved from empires, and by unstable states cut from the Ottoman Empire. [Intellectuals and Society: Part II](https://townhall.com/columnists/thomassowell/2010/01/05/intellectuals_and_society_part_ii)
source: Thomas Sowell, "Intellectuals and Society: Part II," Townhall, January 5, 2010, https://townhall.com/columnists/thomassowell/2010/01/05/intellectuals_and_society_part_ii

prompt: A reform raises welfare benefits but also sharply reduces the payoff to taking an entry-level job. Sowell's incentives lens most naturally asks:

choices.text: What behavior does this reward, and what unintended responses should we expect?
Only whether the reformers meant well
Whether the slogan mentions justice
Whether experts feel unconstrained by trade-offs

explain: Throughout Basic Economics and his policy writing, he treats incentives as drivers of outcomes, independent of stated goals. In a 22 April 2014 column he names what the welfare rules reward. Unprecedented numbers of Americans were on the food-stamp program and living off government disability payments, because making it unnecessary for many people to work means fewer people work. Most of the households in the bottom 20 percent of income earners had nobody working, and there were more heads of household working full-time and year-round in the top 5 percent than in the bottom 20 percent. Someone receiving housing subsidies and food subsidies can lose more in benefits than they gain in income by taking a legitimate, visible job. He puts the case as a $10,000 rise in income that costs $15,000 in benefits, more than the equivalent of a 100 percent tax rate, which even millionaires do not pay. See [The High Cost of Liberalism: Part III](https://capitalismmagazine.com/2014/04/high-cost-liberalism-part-iii/).
source: Thomas Sowell, "The High Cost of Liberalism: Part III," Capitalism Magazine, 22 April 2014, https://capitalismmagazine.com/2014/04/high-cost-liberalism-part-iii/

prompt: Commentators say a minority community's problems must be explained only by race or only by outsider oppression. A Sowellian alternative emphasis would be:

choices.text: Ignore the history of discrimination entirely
Assume all cultures produce identical results under identical laws
Replace cultural discussion with slogans only
Also examine culture, human capital, and internal patterns, not race as destiny and not a single external cause for every gap

explain: Black Rednecks and White Liberals and Discrimination and Disparities stress culture and multiple causes. They reject both a biological destiny story and a discrimination-only story. In a column reprinted on 6 August 2020, Sowell names the cases. In the early 19th century even the poorest Jews in the Russian Empire saw to it that their daughters could read, and their homes had at least ten books, while Thomas Jefferson complained that there was not a single bookstore where he lived, and Frederick Law Olmsted found that antebellum Southern plantation owners seldom had many books. Mid-18th century Scotland had lending libraries in its towns. Arriving in Harlem in the 1930s, Sowell did not know what a public library was until Eddie Mapp took him to one, while Jewish immigrants had already used those libraries and their children had entered the elite public high schools and free city colleges. Two middle-class couples later took young relatives out of the ghetto to educate them. One youngster had an IQ two standard deviations above the mean. Both returned to the ghetto life they came from. Sowell writes that it was not genetics and it was not discrimination. See [Economic Inequality, Culture and Capitalism](https://capitalismmagazine.com/2020/08/economic-inequality-culture-and-capitalism/).
source: Thomas Sowell, "Economic Inequality, Culture and Capitalism," Capitalism Magazine, 6 August 2020, originally published 2016, https://capitalismmagazine.com/2020/08/economic-inequality-culture-and-capitalism/

prompt: In Basic Economics, what does Sowell argue a wage floor above the market rate tends to do to less-skilled workers?

choices.text: Remove any trade-off between the wage and the number of jobs
Raise the cost of their labor and reduce the jobs and hours employers offer them
Automatically raise employment because those workers spend more
Affect only workers who already earn far above the floor

explain: He treats a legal wage above what a worker's output is worth to an employer as a price that can leave that worker unemployed or with fewer hours. In Basic Economics he names who is hit. Minimum wage laws were once advocated expressly to reduce the competition of particular minorities, whether Japanese in Canada during the 1920s or blacks in the United States and South Africa at about the same time. The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 was, for practical purposes, repealed by wartime inflation in the 1940s, because even unskilled market wages rose above what the law specified, and the real impact began after 1950, when the first major revision started a series of escalations. From the late nineteenth century past the middle of the twentieth, the labor-force participation rate of American blacks was slightly higher than that of whites, so blacks were just as employable at the wages they received. Those particularly hard hit afterward were black teenage males: even though 1949, the year before those escalations, was a recession year, black male teenage unemployment that year was lower than it was to be at any time during the boom years of the 1960s. See [Basic Economics](https://archive.org/stream/BasicEconomicsACommonSenseGuideToTheEconomy/Sowell%20Basic%20Economics%20A%20Citizen%27s%20Guide%20to%20the%20Economy_djvu.txt).
source: Thomas Sowell, Basic Economics: A Citizen's Guide to the Economy, revised and expanded edition (Basic Books, 2004), https://archive.org/stream/BasicEconomicsACommonSenseGuideToTheEconomy/Sowell%20Basic%20Economics%20A%20Citizen%27s%20Guide%20to%20the%20Economy_djvu.txt

prompt: In Applied Economics, what does thinking beyond stage one mean?

choices.text: Following a policy past its first visible effect to the later reactions it sets off
Stopping the analysis at the first group that benefits
Counting only the budget cost in the first year
Preferring whichever policy has the best opening headline

explain: Sowell describes a Harvard class with Arthur Smithies. Sowell stated the first benefit he expected, and Smithies kept asking what would happen after that, until the later effects looked worse than the problem. Most policy talk, he argues, stops at stage one. In Applied Economics he names the cases. Rent-control laws often fail to control rent, so cities with them end up with higher rents than cities without them, New York and San Francisco being the classic examples. He cites Zimbabwe, where price controls left bread, sugar, and cornmeal vanished, meat virtually nonexistent, and hospital patients dying for lack of basic medical supplies, because suppliers do not supply as much at a lower price. In 1971 Richard Nixon imposed the first peacetime wage and price controls in the country's history, despite economists' advice and his own knowledge of the consequences. Herbert Stein later described cattle withheld from market, chickens drowned, and food-store shelves emptied, effects that showed up after the 1972 election. See [Applied Economics](https://studfile.net/preview/427436/page:2/).
source: Thomas Sowell, Applied Economics: Thinking Beyond Stage One, revised and enlarged edition (Basic Books, 2008), https://studfile.net/preview/427436/page:2/

prompt: Say's Law, the subject of Sowell's Chicago dissertation, is the classical claim that:

choices.text: A legal price floor always raises the quantity demanded
Trade deficits are the only cause of recessions
Demand creates goods even when nothing is produced
Supplies of goods and services create their own demands

explain: Hoover's account of the dissertation uses that gloss: supplies create their own demands. The dissertation itself is a history of the idea, not a claim that modern recessions are impossible. In Say's Law he names the controversies that history is about. Production pays incomes to the suppliers of labor, capital, and land, so the income generated by a given output equals the value of that output, and a larger supply means a larger income with which to demand it. The question the classical argument fought over was whether a nation could have a "general glut." That controversy reached its peak in the 1820s, and the argument erupted again in the Keynesian revolution of the 1930s. Among noneconomists, Robert Owen and Karl Rodbertus argued that workers were left too poor to buy what they had produced and wanted commodities sold according to the labor time in them. Sismondi and Malthus repudiated Owen, and Marx and Engels repudiated Rodbertus. The classical economists who opposed Say's Law were principally Malthus, Sismondi, and Marx. See [Say's Law](https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781400871223_A26113228/preview-9781400871223_A26113228.pdf).
source: Thomas Sowell, Say's Law: An Historical Analysis (Princeton University Press, 1972), publisher preview, https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781400871223_A26113228/preview-9781400871223_A26113228.pdf

prompt: What is Affirmative Action Around the World (2004)?

choices.text: A problem set in undergraduate price theory
A novel about campus life at Cornell
Sowell's comparative study of group-preference policies in several countries
A memoir of his years on the Howard faculty

explain: The book looks at preferential policies outside the United States as well as inside it. The quiz question stops at that project. It does not ask you to recite country-by-country results. The 30 October 2004 Hoover Digest essay drawn from that research names India, Malaysia, Sri Lanka, Nigeria, and the United States. He asks whether the Malay majority are victims of the Chinese minority, the northern Nigerian majority victims of the Ibo minority, or the Sinhalese majority victims of the Tamil minority in Sri Lanka. He also names preferences for untouchables in India, Maori programs in New Zealand, and brahmins in India who set themselves on fire in protest. For the United States in 2001, the essay says more than 16,000 Asian American students scored above 700 on the mathematics SAT, while fewer than 700 black students scored that high, even though blacks outnumbered Asian Americans several times over. See [Affirmative Action around the World](https://www.hoover.org/research/affirmative-action-around-world).
source: Thomas Sowell, "Affirmative Action around the World," Hoover Digest 2004, no. 4, 30 October 2004, https://www.hoover.org/research/affirmative-action-around-world

prompt: In Sowell's comparative work, a middleman minority is a group that:

prompt: What has Sowell argued about Washington's Dunbar High School, earlier called the M Street School?

choices.text: For decades it met or beat national test norms despite poor funding, and success there cannot be waved off by calling the students middle class without evidence
It was a wealthy boarding school that never enrolled the children of laborers
It opened in 1975 as the nation's first charter school
Its record proves school spending was the only thing that ever mattered

explain: He followed the school from 1870 to 1955. It was renamed Dunbar in 1916. In his telling, 1899 test scores beat two of the city's three white academic high schools, and parent occupations in 1892-93 included many laborers, not a doctor-heavy middle class. Educators who dismissed the record as middle class, he wrote, had not checked. The January 1999 Imprimis essay prints the count: of 83 known parental occupations in 1892-93, 51 were laborers and one was a doctor. He names an early principal, Mary Jane Patterson, Oberlin class of 1862, the first black woman to receive a college degree in the United States. As of 1916, six of the nine black students from the entire country at Amherst College were from Dunbar. He also names Allison Davis of the University of Chicago as the first black full professor at a major university to come from the school, and a later ghetto elementary school, P.S. 91 in Brooklyn, where most grades scored at or above national norms. See [Minority Schools and the Politics of Education](https://imprimis.hillsdale.edu/minority-schools-and-the-politics-of-education/).

prompt: What is the job of the papers in Education: Assumptions versus History?

choices.text: Replace history courses with one vocational track for every student
Argue that schools should ignore evidence and follow expert intention
Tell the story of his years as a high-school principal
Test fashionable assumptions about schools and universities against historical and contemporary evidence

explain: The Hoover Institution Press description says the papers test assumptions behind education policies against the record. Topics include affirmative action, race and IQ debates, tuition tax credits, and academic tenure. The preface and the essay "Race and IQ," in a Hoover Institution Press preview, name the comparisons. World War I Army tests and 1920s surveys put average IQs for Italians, Poles, and Greeks in the 80s, and sometimes the 70s. Carl Brigham, originator of the College Board Scholastic Aptitude Test, read the low scores of soldiers of Polish and Russian ancestry as evidence against the belief that Jews were highly intelligent. Sowell writes that Chinese Americans and Japanese Americans also once scored below the U.S. average and later exceeded it, and that Italian American and Polish American averages rose by 20 to 25 points. He cites Sandra Scarr of the University of Minnesota, who found that black orphans raised in white families had an average IQ of 106, and an all-black Washington school that had an average IQ of 111 in 1939, within walking distance of the Supreme Court. He also names low scores in isolated canal-boat communities in England and in the Hebrides. The preview does not print the name Dunbar for that Washington school. See [Education: Assumptions versus History](https://www.everand.com/book/897463156/Education-Assumptions-versus-History-Collected-Papers).
source: Thomas Sowell, Education: Assumptions versus History: Collected Papers, Hoover Institution Press, 1985, essay "Race and IQ," ebook preview, https://www.everand.com/book/897463156/Education-Assumptions-versus-History-Collected-Papers

explain: The books describe children who talk late and often show unusual memory, music, or mathematical interest. Sowell's son John was one such child. He reports that the pattern is often mistaken for a broader developmental disorder, including autism. His 20 May 1998 column names nuclear physicists Albert Einstein, Edward Teller, and Richard Feynman of Cal Tech as late talkers who had been thought mentally retarded. He says his own son was almost four before he began to talk and, like the children parents then wrote him about, showed unusual ability in mathematics, chess, and computers, and a remarkable memory. His research on 46 late-talking children found that the great majority were boys and that the average age at which they talked was four. He writes that traits common among high-IQ children were enough for some evaluators to label them autistic. The column does not print the son's name. A Kirkus review of the Basic Books edition, dated 6 August 1997, calls him John and says he later became a computer scientist. See [Smart but silent](https://jewishworldreview.com/cols/sowell052098.html).
source: Thomas Sowell, "Smart but silent," Jewish World Review, 20 May 1998, https://jewishworldreview.com/cols/sowell052098.html . prompt: How has Sowell treated government wage and price controls?

choices.text: As something that works only when economists oppose it
As a policy he urged President Nixon to adopt
As a recurring temptation that can sound good at first and then produce shortages and other damage
As a tool that ended scarcity both in ancient Rome and in the 1970s

explain: On the National Humanities Medal site he points to Nixon's wage and price controls, which he says sounded good and then failed, and to similar controls under the emperor Diocletian. In Basic Economics he names what those controls did. A contemporary of Diocletian wrote that after the emperor's price decrees, "people brought provisions no more to markets." Under the Nixon administration, price controls led to declining supplies, and more American cattle were exported, mostly to Canada, instead of being sold in the controlled U.S. market. He writes that the results were essentially the same under Diocletian, in the Soviet Union under the Communists, and in Ghana under Nkrumah. Under American wartime price controls still in effect just after World War II, a 1946 survey reported that approximately 85 percent of stores had no veal and more than four-fifths were without pork loins, ham, or bacon. Within one month after those controls ended, employment in meat-packing plants rose from 93,000 to 163,000. See [Basic Economics](https://archive.org/stream/BasicEconomicsACommonSenseGuideToTheEconomy/Sowell%20Basic%20Economics%20A%20Citizen%27s%20Guide%20to%20the%20Economy_djvu.txt).

prompt: In Basic Economics, how does Sowell connect laws such as the Davis-Bacon Act to black workers?

choices.text: He argues federal wage floors shut out black workers who had been competing by accepting lower pay
He argues Davis-Bacon was written to expand black employment on federal construction
He argues a legal wage floor cannot change who gets hired
He argues the act applied only to farms in Puerto Rico

explain: He groups Davis-Bacon (1931) with the National Industrial Recovery Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act as government wage mandates. In a 17 September 2013 column he names the case the supporters of Davis-Bacon used, and the same device elsewhere. In 1925 a minimum wage law in British Columbia was passed with the intent and effect of pricing Japanese immigrants out of jobs in the lumbering industry. A Harvard professor of that era referred approvingly to Australia's minimum wage law as a means of protecting the white Australian's standard of living from the competition of the Chinese, who were willing to work for less. In South Africa during apartheid, white labor unions urged that a minimum wage be applied to all races so black workers could not take jobs from white unionized workers by working for less than the union scale. Some supporters of the Davis-Bacon Act of 1931, which he calls the first federal minimum wage law, used that rationale: Southern construction companies, using non-union black workers, were able to come north and underbid companies that used unionized white labor. See [Minimum Wage Madness: Part II](https://capitalismmagazine.com/2013/09/minimum-wage-madness-part-ii/).
source: Thomas Sowell, "Minimum Wage Madness: Part II," Capitalism Magazine, 17 September 2013, https://capitalismmagazine.com/2013/09/minimum-wage-madness-part-ii/

prompt: What is Social Justice Fallacies (2023)?

choices.text: A 1975 textbook of input-output tables
The memoir published as A Personal Odyssey
A novel he coauthored with Milton Friedman
Sowell's book on arguments made in the name of social justice

explain: Basic Books published it in 2023. It is a late entry in the same project as his policy books: take claims that travel under a moral label and ask what the evidence and the trade-offs are. A 15 September 2023 Hoover account of his Uncommon Knowledge interview on the book names the cases he used. He argues that racism is not the primary cause of poverty in part because there are white populations, often labeled a privileged group, still living in squalor in the United States. He says the black poverty rate dropped from 87 percent to 47 percent from 1940 to the 1960s, and that this progress came before the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Looking back to the 1940s, the proportion of black households led by a single parent was 17 percent, and after the social welfare programs of the 1960s took effect that figure quadrupled to 68 percent. He treats the 1964 Act as having guaranteed constitutional rights, ended discriminatory practices in hiring, and prohibited segregation in public places, while saying those welfare programs worked to the detriment of black populations. See [Thomas Sowell Launches New Book, Social Justice Fallacies](https://www.hoover.org/news/thomas-sowell-launches-new-book-social-justice-fallacies-uncommon-knowledge).

prompt: Economists’ estimated decade tradeoff of a baby airplane-seat mandate:

choices.text: Save 60 babies, lose 1 adult, $7.2M
Save 1 baby life, lose ~60 other lives, ~$72M
Save 10 babies, lose 10 drivers, ~$720M
No lives changed; only higher fares

explain: Sowell says economists estimated that a decade of a baby airplane-seat mandate would save 1 baby life, lose about 60 other lives, and cost about $72 million. Outside research. McKenzie and Lee, Cato Briefing Paper No. 11, 30 August 1990, [Ending the Free Airplane Rides of Infants](https://web.archive.org/web/20020803113933/http://www.cato.org/pubs/briefs/bp-011.html), say driving was at least 30 times deadlier per mile than scheduled airline travel. They cite a 4 June 1990 Department of Transportation draft that mandatory seats could have prevented at most one infant airline death since 1978. Their model estimates just under 5 extra highway deaths a year. Note 23 sets that against 1 airline life over 12 years, which is 60 highway deaths for each airline life saved. The paper puts extra wreck losses at $6 million a year. It does not print $72 million. Twelve times the annual wreck-loss figure is $72 million, which is how the quiz dollar amount can be reconstructed, and it remains an inference. A December 2011 FAA update, [child-restraint tradeoff PDF](https://web.archive.org/web/20161118013447/https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/docs/2011-12-29-child-restraint-update.pdf), uses 72 as extra transportation deaths over 10 years, against about 1 infant life over 10 to 15 years. The FAA's 1995 report to Congress, summarized in the [26 August 2005 Federal Register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2005/08/26/05-16783/child-restraint-systems), estimated about five infant lives saved on aircraft over 10 years and still found a net increase in deaths.
source: Thomas Sowell, Institution for World Capitalism, Jacksonville, 14 October 1993. Alvarism upload https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wh-qTnq-cwM , auto-captions about 6:01.

This pass did not find two highway deaths or about 52 replacement-power deaths. A 15 November 1980 letter in the NRC docket estimates more than 173 premature deaths by that date from coal power replacing idle Unit 1. See [NRC ML19340C816](https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML1934/ML19340C816.pdf). That figure is not 52, and it is one writer's proration, not an official death count.
